source_review.notes: Checked current Linux kernel and man-pages documentation, OCI, QEMU, Firecracker, gVisor and Kata project documentation, and NIST container-security guidance for process, container, application-kernel, VM and microVM boundaries. All ten cited URLs returned HTTP 200 after normal redirects; mechanism descriptions, vendor design claims, abstract models, operational guidance and comparative assurance remain separately scoped.

evidence: Checked design-tuple, principal, boundary, interface, TCB, resource, evidence, attacker, asset, attack-path, memory, working-set, overhead, packing and readiness-stage notation.
Reviewed existential boundary coverage over attack paths, integer packing bounds and serial readiness sums with their stated assumptions.
notation_and_syntax.notes: Notation separates deployed configuration, threat-path review, idealized capacity and staged startup rather than collapsing dimensions into one score.

evidence: Executed idealized packing for 57,344 MiB available, 512 MiB workload working set and boundary overheads 0, 80, 128 and 1,024 MiB.
Confirmed integer bounds 112, 96, 89 and 37; independently recomputed the exercise's zero-, 128-MiB- and 1-GiB-overhead cases.
numerical_recomputation.notes: The deterministic computation validates integer division only; it implements no real sharing, fragmentation, overcommit, reservation, performance, reliability, density or security behavior.

evidence: Re-derived the deployed-isolation tuple and the review obligation that each enumerated attacker-to-asset path contain an enforced boundary with satisfied assumptions.
Checked dimensionally consistent memory packing and serial readiness equations, including the need for a dependency graph when stages overlap or costs are deferred.
symbolic_recomputation.notes: The expressions are architecture-review tools and do not claim exhaustive attack-path enumeration, real density prediction, independent security factors or complete lifecycle timing.

evidence: Reviewed privileged containers, compatibility ABIs, guest root, virtual devices, VMM helpers, passthrough, IOMMU assumptions, application-kernel gaps and nested boundaries.
Reviewed tenant grouping, memory denominators, cold versus warm startup, host-side resource work, shared storage, metadata, control planes, hardware side channels, snapshots and external leases.
boundary_and_adversarial_cases.notes: Principal, shared-kernel, guest-kernel, device, helper, control-plane, resource, data, hardware and lifecycle boundaries receive distinct treatment.

evidence: Traced workload instructions through host syscalls, application-kernel interception or guest kernel and virtual devices to host services.
Verified TCB ownership, bypass paths, scoped root, complete resource accounting, artifact patching, identity, state transitions and equivalent benchmark denominators.
invariant_checking.notes: The chapter treats isolation choice as an attacker-path and operational-system design, not a ranking of container, sandbox or VM product categories.

evidence: Reviewed every stated attacker-to-asset path for a concrete enforced crossing and included its enforcing hardware and software in the TCB.
Constructed counterexamples for container-as-primitive, VM-as-universally-stronger, microVM-as-kernelless, nesting-as-independent-doubling, passthrough-as-only-performance and snapshot-as-backup.
proof_review.notes: The chapter supplies reusable isolation-selection obligations, not a formal proof of Linux, KVM, QEMU, Firecracker, gVisor, Kata, OCI, a workload, product or tenant boundary.

evidence: Audited uses of isolated, shared, protected, trusted, secure, stronger, contained, compatible, confidential, available and equivalent.
Confirmed kernel mechanisms, project design descriptions, simplified equations, examples, operational recommendations and assurance limits remain separately labeled.
proof_sketch_labeling.notes: Hardware virtualization is not labeled universally stronger, a microVM is not labeled a container, application-kernel compatibility is not labeled identical, escape resistance is not labeled availability and packing is not labeled security.

evidence: artifacts/snippets/OS-090/report.json records source, expected and actual output, stderr, exit status, toolchain and environment for idealized memory packing.
Reviewed required host, guest, VMM, sandbox, device, passthrough, policy, cgroup, image, credential, storage, network, control-plane, startup, resident-memory and lifecycle evidence.
empirical_evidence_labeling.notes: The passing toy establishes five arithmetic outputs only; it provides no evidence for real density, performance, compatibility, isolation, security, side-channel resistance or recovery.

conceptual_review.notes: Reviewed process, container, application-kernel, VM and microVM designs by concrete enforcement boundary, exposed interface, TCB, shared services, resource policy and evidence.

practitioner_review.notes: Reviewed implementable concerns including tenant grouping, kernel exposure, device models, passthrough, VMM jailing, compatibility, nesting, memory, startup, cgroups, shared storage, control planes, side channels, patching, observability and snapshots. Internal practitioner-oriented review only.

pedagogical_review.notes: Verified progression from threat model and mechanism taxonomy through interfaces, nesting and tenant units to capacity, lifecycle, control planes and evidence, followed by twelve obligations, sixteen trade-offs, twenty-six misconceptions, ten examples and five complete exercises.

limitations: Internal evidence record only; no external operating-systems academic, Linux KVM or container maintainer, QEMU, Firecracker, gVisor, Kata or OCI maintainer, virtualization engineer, security reviewer, independent-verification or certification review is claimed.
